Reinforcement learning taught this robot to run in a way no human does, and there's a reason for it. People swing their arms mostly to cancel the twist that every stride sends through the torso. On a robot, the arm is motors, gears and wiring, and swinging it hard means high torque again and again for an entire lap. The forward lean moves the center of mass out in front of the feet, where speed wants it. For a two-legged robot, that means less effort spent staying upright and more of every step turned into forward motion. Interested in AI? Follow @AiEvolutio58513 and never fall behind. Banger paper from Google DeepMind on co-evolving an agent's harness and its weights. (bookmark it) If you already log your harness changes and results, those logs can become training data for the model running inside the harness. This is a nice paper from Google showing how to do this co-evolution. Specifically, they propose Evo2, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. How it works: One policy plays two roles. As a Proposer, it writes edits to its own harness, and as a Reflector, it diagnoses what each edit changed. Those edits and their outcomes then become training data for both roles, using SFT followed by interleaved GRPO. The result: Evo2 reaches 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 82.1% on Polyglot, against 41.0% and 62.6% for the strongest baselines. The harness part alone moves a GPT-5-mini agent from 24.4% to 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified. The evolved harnesses also transfer to other benchmarks without further evolution. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13025 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/evo-2-evolving-the-evolver-through-weight-harness-co-evolution-2610.13025

I came across a company called @ZyG_Edge doing something pretty wild: predicting whether an ecom brand with proven early success can grow 10x and become a category leader. And then executing that growth end to end. What caught my attention is the model they’ve built: with around $10K in live testing, they can assess a brand’s potential to scale. For a brand already selling $1M+ a year, that’s a pretty valuable question to answer: you know people want your product, but how big could this become, and how do you get there? First, ZyG’s AI analyzes your market, competitors, ads, reviews, pricing, and more to identify your strongest growth opportunities. That’s your ZyGnal, and it’s free. Then comes the Marketability Test. ZyG builds and tests positioning, creative, offers, and storefronts with real customers, using around $10K in media spend. And ZyG is now offering a fully funded test - $10K - to the 500 most promising brands, based on their ZyGnal. Their model uses the results - CAC, ROAS, predicted LTV, and other key metrics - to assess what your economics could look like at scale. Those findings feed into your ZyG Score, giving you a clearer picture of your breakout potential. And for brands with strong results, ZyG can then execute the growth end-to-end, from storefront optimization and creative to customer acquisition and retention. With a free ZyGnal and an opportunity for a fully-funded Marketability Test, it seems like a pretty obvious win for most brands. You already gave the LLM the answer. So why is it writing it out from scratch? Introducing a new AI model architecture: Constrained Decoding Models (CDMs) LLMs were built to write. Most production workloads just need an answer: fast, consistent, and affordable. CDMs are purpose-built for 1 task each. They read your input once and skip the token-by-token generative loop that makes LLMs slow and expensive. Not just a decision model, but a family of 3 CDMs live today: • Classify: define your labels and get back a calibrated probability + reason for each. Used for routing, tagging, and intent detection. • Extract: describe the entities in natural language and get back well-formed JSON with confidence scores + citations. Used for web scraping, document processing, and PII redaction. • Summarize: pass in long text, images, or PDFs and get back a consistent summary under 1,000 tokens. Used for context compaction, metadata generation, and transcript digests. Built for production: • 1M tokens of multimodal (text + image) input, 31x larger than Jev • 77.2% on DecisionBench vs Jev's 72% • 200x faster, 467x cheaper than frontier LLM APIs • $0.05/M input tokens. Learn to build custom harnesses, folks! Here is an impressive paper showing the impact of a good custom harness on long-context work. GLM-5.3-Flash goes from 4.4% to 61.1% exact match on OfficeQA Pro V2 with the same model. The authors report that the gain comes from the harness. The model-agnostic harness name is LongHarness, built for corpora of 100M tokens and more. Why it works: Standard agent harnesses keep evidence and conclusions mixed into one growing chat history. Retrieval keeps expanding without closing the actual gap, and corrections stop reaching the answer. LongHarness stores both as explicit state. Open conclusions decide what to retrieve next, and each new piece of evidence confirms or revises the conclusions that asked for it. On the same benchmark, it beats Claude Code by 12.1 points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13075 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/longharness-advancing-agentic-reasoning-over-100m-token-corpora-via-stateful-evi-2610.13075

Using Gemini 4 makes you realize how many other models must be distilling Claude/GPT (or using a similar training pipeline). It feels quite different than other models.

I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base. Here is a fun example: "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end" Astra Max in Codex: https://formwork-city.netlify.app/Fable 5.1 Max in Code: https://brut-city.netlify.app/ Argon in Antigravity: https://rainbow-panda-689e6b.netlify.app/

Just had a chance to host a chat with @emollick about his upcoming book, Co-Existence. It is going to be a hit and is full of practical insights on AI. There will be many positive reviews of the ideas, but let me suggest three non-obvious meta-reasons to read it sooner rather than later: 1. How to work (co-exist?) with AI. Every so often, Ethan pulls back the curtain and describes how he uses AI in the book writing process. You get a peek into specific techniques and, more importantly, the mindset that will make someone successful. 2. The Mollick production function. The book is long enough to give Ethan breathing room to show why he's such a different thinker and fun to hang out with. He actually plays with the tools for long enough to get a finger-feel for what's possible (that's why he is texting at 2 am!); he constantly conceptualizes what he's encountering (jagged frontier, leadership-crowd-lab, the multi-player 2x2, etc.), pushing the ideas to their logical (and often uncomfortable) conclusion; and he ruthlessly throws away ideas when they no longer match the facts on the ground (especially important as everything changes so rapidly). 3. Common knowledge. In this time of hyper-personalized bubbles, we forget the value in having a shared set of stories, frameworks, and ideas. Ethan's book is going to be read by everyone from CEOs to ambitious high schoolers. The book is going to be referenced at many business meetings and holiday dinners so you might as well join in the fun early so you can give a knowing look when someone tells his escalator vs eschaton story, explains the best reasons not to use AI, or debates StrongDM-style software factories.
